The regulation says substance dependence is disqualifying "except where there is established clinical evidence, satisfactory to the Federal Air Surgeon, of recovery, including sustained total abstinence from the substance(s) for not less than the preceding 2 years," which is the standard for qualifying without a Special Issuance. The pilot Step Down Plan says "Permanent abstinence from mind and mood altering substances is required for the duration of the flying career." Your monitoring clock, which the FAA calls Time in Phase, starts on the date your initial Special Issuance is authorized, and if you relapse or an authorization is withdrawn at any time it resets to the date of the most recent Authorization letter.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, ADHD Disposition Table

requirementText: If you have stopped ADHD medication, the FAA's interval is 90 days. Its ADHD disposition table states you "must be off the medication(s) for 90 days before testing and evaluation," and the pilot-facing Standard Track sheet repeats that you "must have discontinued ADHD medication at least 90 days prior to testing." Schedule the neuropsychological evaluation so it falls after that 90th day. If you are currently taking ADHD medication, or stopped within the past 90 days, the FAA places you in a defer row and asks for one document: "the most recent detailed, clinical progress note from the prescribing physician which identifies the diagnosis and treatment plan." Ask for that actual clinical note, not a patient portal after-visit summary. The FAA counts any use inside this window, including as-needed (PRN) use and medication prescribed for a non-ADHD reason. Whether the medication can be safely discontinued is your treating physician's decision.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, Standard Track FAA ADHD Evaluation, General Information for Pilots and ATCS

requirementText: Which testing you need depends on your track. If you have had no ADHD symptoms, treatment, medication or instability in the past four years and no other psychiatric diagnosis, current or historical, the FAA's Fast Track is a records review and clinical interview with no test battery (the FAA allows one exception, for anxiety, depression and related conditions that qualify for their own Fast Track pathway). Testing can still be added: the FAA lists a battery as required if a clear determination cannot be reached on the Fast Track, if your AME or the evaluator has concerns, or if the FAA requests it. Otherwise you are on the Standard Track, where the FAA states the "evaluation and testing must be performed IN-PERSON by a HIMS neuropsychologist within 90 days of the AME exam." The FAA does not publish the test list. It states the "testing specifications required by the FAA are listed on an FAA secure site used by professionals with training regarding the specifications," so your HIMS neuropsychologist obtains them directly and there is no public battery for you to look up. Standard Track testing also requires a drug screen, and the timing is unforgiving: "complete a urinalysis for amphetamines and methylphenidate within 24 hours after completing testing." Set the lab order up before your testing day. The FAA tells pilots to "verify if the evaluating HIMS Neuropsychologist has the ability to order the urinalysis," because that varies by state, and if not to "coordinate with your AME or your primary care physician to order the laboratory test." Order both tests, because the FAA warns "they are two different tests/different test batteries," and get the lab paperwork itself, because "actual laboratory results are required (not clinical summary of results)" and "testing data cannot be used without the supporting urinalysis."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, FAA ADHD Document Checklist

requirementText: This is the evaluator's report, and the FAA is specific about who writes it and what must reach them first. On the Fast Track the evaluator is a "doctoral level (PhD or PsyD) psychologist or neuropsychologist with training and experience in the evaluation of ADHD." On the Standard Track it must be an FAA HIMS Neuropsychologist. The FAA's ADHD Document Checklist lists what you send that evaluator before the appointment: pharmacy records within the last four years; medical records for the ADHD diagnosis and treatment; records from any psychiatrist, psychologist, therapist, school counselor, education specialist or teacher, speech therapist or occupational therapist; records for any non-ADHD condition treated with an ADHD medication; driver's license records from every state that licensed you in the past four years; academic records including all transcripts through your highest grade or degree, any Section 504 Plan, any IEP and any record of academic or occupational accommodations; and a personal statement, "typed, signed, and dated," covering every item on the FAA ADHD Personal Statement Guidelines. The FAA adds: "make a copy of all the records above as you will also need to bring a copy to your AME to upload into your FAA record." The report itself "must be performed within 90 days of the AME exam." If the evaluator asks for your entire FAA medical file, FAA Form 8065-2 has the agency send those records directly to the psychologist or neuropsychologist. On the Fast Track, also ask the evaluator to complete the FAA ADHD Summary form; the FAA says it is "NOT required, however, it will help to streamline and significantly DECREASE FAA review time." Read that against the disposition table, because leaving it out changes which row you are in rather than just how fast the mail moves. Row A is the ISSUE row, and its own note reads: "If FAA ADHD Summary is not provided, any 'YES' answers, any AME concerns, or unable to verify history, go to Row B." Row B is DEFER, and it "requires HIMS neuropsychology evaluation and testing" completed "in person by a HIMS neuropsychologist." The FAA's Fast Track sheet also tells you to coordinate with your AME so everything is uploaded to the FAA within 14 days, and warns that "partial or incomplete packages will NOT be reviewed and will cause a DELAY."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI Asthma

requirementText: A current medical status report on your asthma from your treating physician. The FAA's AASI protocol for asthma names what it has to cover: your current medical status "that addresses frequency of attacks and whether the attacks have resulted in emergency room visits or hospitalizations." Make sure the report speaks to both of those directly, the frequency and the emergency room or hospital history. Your Authorization letter also comes with attachments that specify what your treating physician must provide for the reissue determination, so check the report against those. Separately, the same protocol reminds your Examiner to caution you to cease flying with any exacerbation, as warned in 14 CFR 61.53.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI Asthma

requirementText: The name and dosage of every asthma medication you take, covering both what you use to treat an attack and what you take to prevent one, together with your physician's comment on side effects. The FAA's wording is "the name and dosage of medication(s) used for treatment and/or prevention with comment regarding side effects." Two parts of that are easy to miss: preventive or maintenance inhalers count even though you do not reach for them during an attack, and the comment on side effects is part of the item rather than an optional extra. You bring this to your Examiner, and a reissue at the desk is conditional rather than automatic: "Examiners may re-issue an airman medical certificate under the provisions of an Authorization, if the applicant provides the following." Two of the FAA's own deferral triggers turn on what is in this list, so they are worth knowing before your exam. The FAA states: "The Examiner must defer to the AMCD or Region if: The symptoms worsen; There has been an increase in frequency of emergency room, hospital, or outpatient visits; The FEV1 is less than 70% predicted value; The applicant requires 3 or more medications for stabilization; or The applicant is taking steroids doses equivalent to more than 20mg of prednisone per day," and it links a steroid conversion calculator for that last one. Note the FAA's trigger is three or more medications that the applicant "requires ... for stabilization," which is your physician's clinical judgment rather than a tally you do yourself from this list.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI Asthma

requirementText: Pulmonary function testing results, but only when they are actually called for. The FAA lists this among the items you provide at reissue as "Results of pulmonary function testing, if deemed necessary," so it is not an automatic test. What the FAA is specific about is recency: when the testing is needed, it asks for results performed within the last 90 days, so an older test already sitting in your file will not cover it. Worth asking your Examiner ahead of your exam whether they need one this time, because a 90 day window means it has to be scheduled close to the appointment.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI COPD

requirementText: Bring two test results, both performed no more than 90 days before your AME exam: a Pulmonary Function Test (PFT) and a 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT). Attach copies of both. The FAA's stated PFT threshold is a post-bronchodilator FEV1 greater than 60 percent predicted, and the AME Guide directs your AME to defer to the FAA if FEV1 is less than 60 percent. For the 6MWT the FAA publishes its own Six-Minute Walk Test Result Sheet for your treating provider to complete, requires the test be done to American Thoracic Society guidelines, and directs your AME to defer if the results show a 4 percent drop in SpO2 from baseline or less than 400 meters walked. The result sheet is in the AME Guide under Disease Protocols. Your AME uploads both results to the FAA for your file.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, COPD Status Summary

requirementText: The FAA accepts either a completed COPD Status Summary with every item answered YES, or a current, detailed Clinical Progress Note that addresses each item. Have your pulmonologist, or whichever physician manages your COPD, complete it no more than 90 days before your AME exam. The form's items are: GOLD stage 1 or 2a and stable, with no hospitalizations and no moderate or severe exacerbations in the past year; resting oxygen saturation of 96 percent or higher; your PFT result; your 6-minute walk test result; your medications; and a written explanation of any NO answer, for which the form directs your physician to attach a current, detailed Clinical Progress Note. The AME Guide directs your AME to defer to the FAA if resting oxygen saturation is 95 percent or lower. Download the COPD Status Summary from the FAA's COPD page and take it to the appointment.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI COPD

requirementText: The FAA does not ask for a separate medication list document for COPD. Medications appear inside two FAA forms instead. On the COPD Status Summary, item 5 has the physician who manages your COPD confirm you are treated with three or fewer COPD medications, not counting a rescue inhaler (the FAA's own example is Trelegy plus albuterol), and that oral prednisone or similar is not needed and not used daily. On the Six-Minute Walk Test Result Sheet, item 2 asks your provider to list all current cardiopulmonary medications. The AME Guide directs your AME to defer to the FAA if you are taking 4 or more medications for COPD or are on daily oral steroid use. Bring your current names and doses to the appointment so both can be filled in accurately.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI for Venous Thromboembolism (VTE), DVT, PE and Hypercoagulopathies

requirementText: A summary of your medical condition since your last FAA medical examination. The FAA requires it to include "a statement regarding any further episodes of VTE (DVT, PE) or other complication of hypercoagulopathy," your future treatment plan, and your prognosis. If you take a NOAC or DOAC such as Xarelto, Eliquis, Pradaxa or Savaysa, the FAA additionally asks you to obtain a statement from your treating or prescribing physician giving details of the underlying condition, how well you tolerate the medication including whether you have had side effects, any bleeding episodes that required medical attention, and any occurrence or recurrence of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. The FAA publishes no stability or recurrence free waiting period for reissue under this Authorization. It does instruct your AME to defer to the FAA's Aerospace Medical Certification Division or Regional Flight Surgeon, rather than reissue at the exam, if you "develop emboli, thrombosis, bleeding, or any other cardiac or neurologic condition previously not diagnosed or reported."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI for Venous Thromboembolism (VTE), DVT, PE and Hypercoagulopathies

requirementText: The name and dosage of every medication you take to treat or prevent clots, with a comment on side effects if you have had any. The FAA's wording is "the name and dosage of all medication(s) used for treatment and/or prevention with comment regarding side effects, if any," so medication you take preventively counts, not only what you take for an active clot. The side effect comment carries weight at the exam: the FAA instructs your AME to defer to its Aerospace Medical Certification Division or Regional Flight Surgeon, rather than reissue, if you "experienced any side effects or bleeding episodes requiring medical attention." If you take warfarin (Jantoven), the FAA's Anticoagulants page also asks that the treating physician's status report cover your "drug dose history and schedule."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI for Venous Thromboembolism (VTE), DVT, PE and Hypercoagulopathies

requirementText: This one applies only if you take warfarin (Jantoven). The FAA asks you to "obtain a minimum of monthly International Normalized Ratio (INR) results for the immediate prior 6 months," so bring at least one INR value per month covering the six months immediately before your exam. The FAA instructs your AME to defer to its Aerospace Medical Certification Division or Regional Flight Surgeon, rather than reissue at the exam, if more than 20 percent of your INR values fall outside the 2.0 to 3.0 range. If you take a NOAC or DOAC such as Xarelto, Eliquis, Pradaxa or Savaysa, the FAA lists no INR test and no other routine anticoagulation lab for reissue. In its place it asks for a statement from your treating or prescribing physician.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI Renal Calculi

requirementText: A current imaging report and a metabolic work-up. The FAA's AASI page for Renal Calculi asks the applicant for "A current report of appropriate imaging study (IVP, KUB, Ultrasound, or Spiral CT Scan) and provide a metabolic work-up, both performed within last 90 days." Both pieces are named, and the 90-day limit applies to both, so a scan or a lab panel from your last renewal does not carry forward. Two of the three situations in which the FAA tells the Examiner to defer instead of reissuing are comparisons against your earlier studies: a retained stone that "has moved when compared to previous evaluations," or one that "has become larger when compared to previous evaluations." Having your prior imaging reports on hand is what makes that comparison possible.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI Renal Calculi

requirementText: A statement from your treating physician. The FAA's AASI page for Renal Calculi names what belongs in it: "A statement from your treating physician regarding the location of the retained stone(s), estimation as to size of stone, and likelihood of becoming symptomatic." Location, estimated size, and likelihood of becoming symptomatic are the three points the FAA asks for, so a general note confirming a history of stones does not answer them. The FAA also instructs the Examiner to defer to the AMCD or Region "If the treating physician comments that the current stone has a likelihood of becoming symptomatic." The same page notes that your Authorization letter "is accompanied by attachments that specify the information that treating physician(s) must provide for the re-issuance determination," so read your own attachments alongside this.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, Item 40. Skin, Skin Cancer disposition table

requirementText: The FAA does not name a specialty for melanoma reports. What it publishes instead is the set of documents that goes to the FAA when your melanoma is first deferred, and the list depends on the depth recorded on your pathology report. For a melanoma 0.75 mm or greater in depth, the FAA's Item 40 Skin Cancer disposition table has your AME "Review and submit the following: Medical records describing the diagnosis and treatment; Pathology report(s); Operative notes; Current status report that includes if any additional lesions, any metastatic disease, any current or future treatment planned; and Current MRI brain." For metastatic melanoma, or melanoma of unknown primary origin, the FAA asks for everything on that list plus a PET scan and copies of any additional testing your treating physician performed. That table is guidance written to your AME and it covers the first submission. Once you hold an Authorization, what you bring to each exam comes from the Authorization letter instead.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI for Melanoma

requirementText: The FAA works from one measurement on your pathology report, the Breslow depth in millimeters, together with whether there is metastasis. Neither the FAA's melanoma AASI page nor its Item 40 Skin Cancer disposition table uses a cancer stage number. The AASI page states: "A Special Issuance or AASI is required for any melanoma which exhibits Breslow Level equal to or deeper than 0.75 mm with or without metastasis," and "A Special Issuance or AASI is required for any metastatic melanoma regardless of Breslow level," and "A melanoma that exhibits a Breslow Level of less than 0.75 mm and no evidence of metastasis may be regular issued." So the document to keep is the pathology report showing the Breslow measurement, the margins, and whether any metastatic disease was found. Even for a melanoma under 0.75 mm the Item 40 table has the reports sent in "for retention in the file," so your AME will ask for them either way.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI for Melanoma

requirementText: The FAA does not publish a follow-up item list for melanoma, and there is no FAA melanoma status form. Its AASI page gives a two item reissue list, and the second item points back at your own paperwork: your AME may reissue if you provide "An Authorization granted by the FAA" and "A current status report performed within 90 days that must include all the required followup items and studies as listed in the Authorization letter and that confirms absence of recurrent disease." So the tests and items that have to be in that report are the ones named in the attachments to your own Authorization letter, and the report has to be dated inside the 90 days before your exam. Two things take the decision away from your AME. The FAA says the Examiner must defer to the AMCD or Region if there has been "any recurrence of the cancer" or if "Any new treatment is initiated."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, Item 41. G-U System, Prostate Conditions disposition table

requirementText: This one applies at the initial decision, before you hold an Authorization. The FAA's prostate cancer disposition table sends one row to a Special Issuance: prostate cancer "with Metastatic disease current OR any time in the past OR Recurrence of disease including a biochemical recurrence (BCR) after prostatectomy," which the FAA marks "DEFER" and "Initial Special Issuance." For that row, the FAA lists what gets submitted for FAA review: a "Current status report from oncologist describing treatment plan, how long the condition has been stable, and prognosis"; a "List of medications and presence or absence of side effects with specific attention to any chemotherapy, steroids, or hormone agents and dates used"; "Treatment records including clinic notes or a summary letter describing initial staging, disease course, locations of metastatic disease, and stability"; "Operative notes and discharge summary, if applicable"; "Pathology report(s), if applicable"; and "Results of MRI/CT or PET scan reports," noting that "In some cases, the actual CDs will be required in DICOM format for FAA review." The FAA adds: "If the airman is currently on radiation or chemotherapy, the treatment course should be completed before medical certification can be considered." If that row does not describe your case, this is not your list. The FAA routes non metastatic prostate cancer elsewhere: a regular issuance if treatment finished five or more years ago with no recurrence, otherwise the CACI Prostate Cancer Worksheet, where "If the requirements are not met, the AME must defer the exam and send the supporting documents to the FAA." The FAA publishes no separate document list for a file that reaches it that way, so work from the attachments to your own Authorization letter, which the FAA says "specify the information that treating physician(s) must provide." Once your Authorization is granted, reissue runs on the shorter AASI list, not this one.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI for Prostate Cancer

requirementText: The FAA's AASI list for prostate cancer names one lab your AME needs each time they reissue under your Authorization: "A current PSA level performed within last 90 days." Collect it inside that 90 day window ahead of your exam rather than earlier in the year. The FAA does not name any other marker, staging paperwork or imaging as a routine reissue item, but its other reissue item is broader ("A current status of the medical condition to include any testing deemed necessary"), so your Authorization attachments can call for more. Your PSA trend also decides whether your AME can reissue at all: the FAA tells the Examiner to defer to the AMCD or Region if "The PSA rises at a rate above 0.75 ng/ml per year."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, AASI for Prostate Cancer

requirementText: At each reissue your AME needs, in the FAA's words, "An Authorization granted by the FAA" and "A current status of the medical condition to include any testing deemed necessary." The FAA publishes no template, form, page count or required specialty for that status report on its prostate cancer AASI page. What it does say is that "The Authorization letter is accompanied by attachments that specify the information that treating physician(s) must provide for the re-issuance determination," so the attachments to your own Authorization letter are the list to work from. Two things stop a desk reissue and send your file back to the FAA: your Examiner must defer to the AMCD or Region if "A new treatment is initiated" or "Any metastasis has occurred."

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, Item 18.i, Stomach, liver, or intestinal trouble

requirementText: The FAA publishes no waiting period, observation period or stability interval after bariatric surgery. It has no AASI, no disease protocol and no row in the Abdomen and Viscera disposition tables, so there is no published interval to document, and a surgical procedure is not something that can recur. What the FAA does name is in Item 18.i of Form 8500-8, Stomach, liver, or intestinal trouble: "If a surgical procedure was done, the applicant must provide operative and pathology reports." Ask your surgeon's office for the operative report and the pathology report and store them here. Anything beyond that is set by the attachments to your own FAA Authorization letter.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, General Information, Authorization for Special Issuance and AASI

requirementText: The AME Guide publishes nothing about what a post-bariatric status report should contain, because bariatric surgery is not a listed condition. The FAA states that "the Authorization letter is accompanied by attachments that specify the information that treating physician(s) must provide for the re-issuance determination," so your own letter is the list. Give those attachments to the physician who follows your surgery and ask for exactly what they name. For an unlisted condition the FAA's guidance to your AME, not to you, is to submit the "most recent detailed Clinical Progress Note(s)" and any related treatment records, so expect a current clinical note to be the core of it.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, Condition Not Listed disposition table

requirementText: The AME Guide specifies no labs for bariatric surgery. There is no AASI, no disease protocol and no CACI worksheet for it, so there is no FAA panel to draw against. The FAA's Condition Not Listed disposition table, which is written for your AME rather than for you, asks for "results of recent testing already performed pertinent to the condition." That is testing you have already had, not a new panel ordered for the FAA. The FAA's Federal Air Surgeon's Medical Bulletin article on bariatric surgery (2023, Volume 58-2) discusses micronutrient deficiency and anemia risk after these procedures but sets no requirement, stating that clear guidelines on "the post-operative management of aeronautical personnel who have undergone such surgery are lacking." Store the labs your bariatric program already draws, plus any named in your Authorization letter, here.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, HIMS AME Checklist, Drug and Alcohol Monitoring Recertification

requirementText: The FAA does not list a monthly report from a sponsor. What it lists monthly are two workplace reports, and only for a pilot holding a first or second class certificate who is employed by an air carrier. The recertification checklist marks both "N/A for third-class," and the certification aid heads the chief pilot row "If the airman is 1st or 2nd class and employed by an air carrier." A chief pilot, flight operations supervisor, or airline management designee reports each month on your performance and competence, crew interaction, mood if available, and the presence or absence of any other concerns. A peer pilot, for example from your employer or ALPA, reports each month and must attest, to the best of their knowledge, to your continued total abstinence from drugs or alcohol. You bring the cumulative monthly reports to the HIMS AME evaluation every 6 months. The FAA's checklist carries an "N/A" answer for both of these items, so if you are not flying for an air carrier there is nothing here for you to obtain. Contact with an AA sponsor appears in the FAA's documents under additional reports and treatment records, which are required only when your Authorization letter specifies them.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, FAA Certification Aid, Drug and Alcohol Monitoring Recertification

requirementText: Testing must be random and unannounced. The FAA says "Urine EtG/EtS, PEth testing or a mobile alcohol monitoring system are preferred," and that "At a minimum, frequency must be 14 tests over a 12-month period," which your HIMS AME may increase. The Step Down Plan sets the minimum by phase: 14 screens in 12 months, or a Soberlink type portable breath monitoring system with facial recognition and cellular transmission, in the Initial and Early phases, and 4 PEth tests in 12 months in the Advanced phase. For dependence on anything other than alcohol, or a polysubstance diagnosis, the Advanced phase minimum is 4 PEth tests and 4 urine drug screens every 12 months. Hair testing is not among the methods the FAA names here. Results go to your HIMS AME with each package, and the FAA requires the HIMS AME to report any positive test to the agency immediately.

envelope.sourceCitation: FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners, HIMS AME Checklist, Drug and Alcohol Monitoring Recertification

requirementText: Two different clocks run here. Attendance is frequent: the Step Down Plan lists attendance at a peer addiction support group such as AA or NA twice weekly in the Initial and Early phases and weekly in the Advanced phase, with aftercare weekly in year one. The counselor's report is less frequent: the recertification checklist requires aftercare counselor reports "every 3 months" for first and second class, and for third class "Per Authorization Letter." The report should say whether you are continuing to participate in abstinence based sobriety, how often you attend, and that the counselor agrees to notify your HIMS AME immediately of any change or deterioration in your condition.

requirementText: This is a yearly report, not a quarterly one. The FAA's recertification checklist says a treating psychiatrist report or HIMS psychiatrist report is "Required EVERY 12 months for ALL CLASSES unless a different time interval is specifically stated in the Authorization Letter," and the checklist lets the AME mark it "Not Due" at the alternate visit, since the HIMS AME evaluation comes around more often. The report should summarize the clinical findings and how you are doing, note any clinical concerns or changes in the treatment plan, give recommendations for additional treatment or monitoring, and state the psychiatrist's agreement to notify the FAA or your AME immediately if your condition changes. Interval treatment records such as clinic or hospital notes go with it, and like every report in the package it must be current within the last 90 days.

requirementText: The FAA asks for this more often than once a year. Its recertification checklist says the HIMS AME face-to-face, in office evaluation is "Required EVERY 6 months for ALL CLASSES," and the certification aid adds that it must be performed by the HIMS AME listed on your Authorization letter. Between those, the checklist refers to "Interval evaluations (every 3 months or as required by Authorization Letter)." The Step Down Plan puts the HIMS AME of record at every 3 months in the Initial and Early phases, where half the visits may be virtual, every 6 months in the Advanced phase, and a HIMS AME of your choice at each exam in the Maintenance phase. The AME signs the checklist, writes the narrative report, and states whether you meet all the requirements of your Authorization letter.

requirementText: The FAA does not publish a monthly report from your treating physician for this protocol. Its HIMS AME Checklist for SSRI recertification lists what actually recurs: the HIMS AME face-to-face, in office evaluation "Required EVERY 6 months for ALL CLASSES," the treating psychiatrist report "Required EVERY 6 months for ALL CLASSES," a Chief Pilot or Air Traffic Manager report "Required EVERY 3 months" (the checklist limits this to commercial pilots holding first or second class certificates, and the FAA's certification aid narrows it to those employed by an air carrier within the last 2 years, marking third class as not applicable), and any additional reports your Authorization letter requires. What the FAA does describe between the 6 month visits is interim contact with your HIMS AME by phone, video, or email, at an interval set "either at the AME's discretion or as required by the Authorization or Special Consideration Letter (every 1-3 months)." Those contacts are not filed on their own. Your HIMS AME summarizes them in the 6 month report. Your own Authorization letter is the authority on how often you check in.
